questions.question: What is the main objective of the Majuli virtual reality case study?
options: An immersive, interactive virtual reality tour of the island's ecological and cultural heritage
A travel-planning tool for booking real visits to satras and villages
A static 360-degree gallery for viewing photographs of the island's towns
A healthcare training environment for rehearsing clinical procedures
questions.explanation: The case study aims to create an immersive, interactive VR tour in which visitors can experience the island's ecological heritage and tangible and intangible cultural heritage.

questions.question: Why does the Majuli virtual tour combine walking with teleportation or a vehicle metaphor?
options: The island is geographically large, so one navigation technique alone may not work well
Walking is required for every immersive virtual reality application
Teleportation alone gives a more realistic sense of movement between towns
A vehicle metaphor is used because the tour contains only indoor spaces
questions.explanation: Because the island's large geographical spread means that a single technique such as walking or teleportation alone may not be good, the tour uses walking within points and teleportation or a vehicle metaphor between points.

questions.question: What creates two levels of extensive content in the Majuli virtual tour?
options: Many geographically spread information points, each containing many points of interest
Two user roles, a guide and a visitor, in the tour
Two separate applications for ecological heritage and cultural heritage
Two display resolutions for desktop and mobile deployment
questions.explanation: The tour has many geographically spread information points, and each information point contains many points of interest, creating two levels of extensive content.

questions.question: Why was resource optimization necessary for the Majuli virtual reality application?
options: Its static 360-degree photographs need to be streamed from a local server
Its navigation system requires a high-refresh-rate display to avoid cybersickness
Its rich multimodal content can be interactively changed and needs far more computation and storage than regular systems can support
Its 3D models require a proprietary processor found only in high-end headsets
questions.explanation: Rendering the application's rich, interactively changed multimodal content has computational and storage requirements far beyond rendering a simple static image, and regular systems cannot support it.

questions.question: Which hardware configuration describes the Oculus Quest 2?
options: A standalone headset and controllers with its own processor and memory, not tethered to a fixed computer
A cardboard housing for a smartphone that displays stereoscopic views
A room-scale augmented reality device that tracks an entire physical room
A high-end graphics workstation connected to an external headset
questions.explanation: The Oculus Quest 2 is a standalone computing device with a headset and handheld controllers, its own processor and memory, and no need for a fixed computer.

questions.question: Why did the Oculus Quest 2 application require resource optimization?
options: Because the full system had to be deployed on a smartphone in cardboard
Because the standalone device has less computing power and storage than a high-end graphics workstation
Because eye tracking devices added extra sensor data and rendering requirements
Because the application stored all images, not videos, on a cloud server
questions.explanation: The Quest 2 has less computing power and storage than a high-end graphics workstation, so reducing size reduces rendering requirements and memory access.

questions.question: When a user selected a video thumbnail in the Oculus Quest 2 video player, where did the application obtain the video?
options: From a smartphone inside a cardboard headset, to reduce local size
From the cloud server, not from local storage
From the headset's local storage, to avoid network latency
From a high-end graphics workstation, to reduce storage requirements
questions.explanation: All videos, not images, were stored in the cloud; when a video thumbnail was selected, the video was loaded from the cloud rather than stored locally.

questions.question: What local benefit did the Oculus Quest 2 deployment gain from moving videos to the cloud?
options: The client needed local video playback to keep the experience realistic
The client size increased because thumbnails were cached locally
The client required a tethered workstation for high-quality video rendering
The client size and associated computations were reduced
questions.explanation: Storing the videos in the cloud reduced the deployed client size and produced a corresponding computational reduction.

questions.question: What network conditions were necessary for cloud-based video-loading on the Oculus Quest 2 to be useful?
options: Compressed images, removed video playback, and smartphone storage
Large local storage, fast memory access, and offline video files
High bandwidth support, network coverage, and minimal latency
A high-end workstation, eye tracking, and haptic feedback
questions.explanation: The cloud-based video-loading optimization required high bandwidth, network coverage, and minimal latency to load high-quality videos in real time.

questions.question: What is a cardboard virtual reality headset?
options: A standalone headset with its own processor and handheld controllers
A glass-based display that overlays virtual objects on the real world
A tethered headset connected to a high-end graphics workstation
A cardboard housing that holds a smartphone displaying stereoscopic views
questions.explanation: A cardboard VR headset is a cardboard housing for a smartphone, and the smartphone's stereoscopic display provides the immersive view.

questions.question: Why did the Majuli VR system need optimization for deployment on a smartphone placed in a cardboard headset?
options: Because the cardboard housing reduced the smartphone's available computing power
Because average smartphones cannot display stereoscopic views
Because the full system depended on a cloud server for video playback
Because its full version's size and computation exceeded what average smartphones typically support
questions.explanation: The full Majuli VR system was too large and computationally demanding for average smartphones, so a resource-constrained deployment required optimization.

questions.question: What optimization strategy was used for the smartphone/cardboard deployment of the Majuli VR system?
options: Videos were stored in the cloud and loaded when selected
The system was moved to a standalone headset with its own processor
Images were compressed and video playback support was retained
Images were compressed and video playback support was removed
questions.explanation: For the smartphone/cardboard version, images were compressed to reduce storage and video playback was removed because most videos could not be used.

questions.question: What trade-off resulted from compressing images and removing video playback in the Majuli smartphone/cardboard system?
options: The system could retain more video content than the full version
The overall size of the system increased
The experience required a high-bandwidth cloud connection
The experience became less realistic than the full version
questions.explanation: Compressing images and removing video support reduced resource use but made the experience less realistic than the full implementation.

questions.question: Which general approach is described as allowing video playback to be retained when an immersive VR system has computational limits?
options: Cloud-based services
Removing some features entirely
Compressing images to reduce storage
Replacing video with static 2D drone shots
questions.explanation: Cloud-based services are identified as an approach that can allow video playback to be retained, whereas compression and feature removal are different trade-offs.

questions.question: What can the NPTEL computer graphics MOOC be used to learn in more detail?
options: The operation of the virtual world generator
The cloud-based loading of videos on a standalone headset
The compression of images for smartphone deployment
The stages of the three-dimensional graphics pipeline
questions.explanation: The NPTEL MOOC on computer graphics is described as a resource for learning more details about the stages of the three-dimensional graphics pipeline.

questions.question: Which resource is the source of the computer graphics topics and can be used to study them in more detail?
options: The Oculus Quest 2 standalone device
The Oxford University Press book on computer graphics
The cloud video storage service
The NPTEL computer graphics MOOC
questions.explanation: The Oxford University Press computer graphics book is identified as the source of the topics and can be used to study them in more detail.

questions.question: Why would the Majuli virtual tour application need different resource optimizations for an Oculus Quest 2 headset and for a smartphone placed in a cardboard virtual reality headset?
questions.reference_answer: The Majuli virtual tour application is almost 10 gigabytes in size because its collected multimodal content is vast, and its interactive videos and animations make rendering much more demanding than rendering a static image. Regular systems cannot support the application, and the Oculus Quest 2 has less computing power and relatively less storage than a high-end graphics workstation, so the Quest 2 application was optimized by storing videos in the cloud and loading them on demand, reducing it to 5.1 gigabytes. The smartphone/cardboard deployment had to compress images and remove video playback because the full system's size and computation exceed what average smartphones typically support. That strategy reduced the overall size of the Majuli virtual reality system to about 0.7 gigabytes.

questions.question: How can cloud-based video loading reduce the storage needed on the Oculus Quest 2 while still depending on network conditions for the Majuli virtual tour?
questions.reference_answer: In the Oculus Quest 2 application, videos were not stored locally because videos take up more storage, and a video is loaded from the cloud when the user selects its thumbnail, reducing the deployed application to 5.1 gigabytes. This cloud-based video loading optimization requires high bandwidth, network coverage, and minimal latency to load high-quality videos in real time. Latency is the time delay between a user's movement and the corresponding change in the virtual world, so if network connectivity issues are not resolved, the cloud-based optimization would not be of much help.

questions.question: How does the three-dimensional graphics pipeline explain why a platform that cannot render the required immersive content cannot host the whole Majuli virtual reality system?
questions.reference_answer: The three-dimensional graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process that computes the intensity values for each pixel, stores them in the frame buffer, and uses them to drive the display mechanism through the video controller. Rendering the Majuli virtual tour application's rich multimodal content involves a computational requirement many times higher than rendering a static image and requires fast storage and retrieval support for real-time interactive rendering. When such rendering cannot be performed on the device, deploying the whole Majuli virtual reality system on that platform is not possible.
